gap.title_en: Baseline-EEG prediction of NF responders and responder-adaptive protocols untested in MCI
gap.description_en: Baseline resting-EEG predictors of self-regulation success (e.g., resting beta1 relative power and alpha node strength) and personalized/adaptive protocols have been studied only in healthy adults aged 41-75 and in subjective cognitive decline. No study has tested, in amnestic MCI, whether pre-registered baseline EEG markers predict who learns to modulate the target band, or whether responder status moderates cognitive benefit versus sham.

supporting_evidence.explanation_en: 48.3% non-responders and baseline beta1 power / alpha node strength predicted self-regulation, but only in healthy 65-75 year olds; authors call for further biomarkers of non-responsiveness.
Identified a non-learner group needing about 5 more sessions and found individualized protocols no better than standard, in SCD rather than MCI.
Review names non-response ('BCI illiteracy') as a central unsolved issue and explicitly calls for NF research in MCI.
DNN-personalized NF beat sham, but in healthy adults aged 41-64 (abstract-only).

counter_evidence.explanation_en: Used per-session calibration and adaptive thresholds in aMCI, but did not analyse responders or predictors of learning.
Individualized the band to each patient's PAF, yet reported no learning or responder analysis and no change in PAF.

gap.why_it_matters_en: If roughly half of older trainees fail to self-regulate, average-effect RCTs in MCI will be diluted and appear null; identifying responders from baseline EEG would allow enrichment, stratified trials and clinically targeted prescription of NF to the MCI patients most likely to benefit.
gap.severity_rationale_en: Non-response plausibly explains inconsistent efficacy across trials, but it is not the sole barrier to establishing efficacy.
gap.novelty_rationale_en: No MCI study in the collection examines responder prediction or responder-moderated outcomes.
gap.feasibility_rationale_en: Requires only baseline resting EEG and session logs added to a standard NF trial; assumes MCI recruitment of about 60-90 patients at a memory clinic.

gap.title_en: No sham-controlled MCI trial verifies target engagement of the trained EEG feature
gap.description_en: Controlled MCI trials report cognitive benefit without showing that the trained EEG feature changed (no PAF or upper-alpha change after sham-controlled alpha NF) or without reporting EEG at all; no study tests whether within-session learning of the target band statistically mediates cognitive change versus sham.

supporting_evidence.explanation_en: Memory improved versus sham but PAF (9.32 to 9.36 Hz) and upper-alpha power did not change; authors note the study was underpowered for EEG.
Reports CANTAB effects but no analysis of change in the trained beta/alpha ratio.
Learned modulation was not frequency-specific and resting EEG did not change, questioning the specificity assumed by protocols.
Calls for reporting self-regulation success and its link to clinical outcomes, which included studies rarely did.

counter_evidence.explanation_en: Showed session-wise beta increase (r=0.746) but in an uncontrolled n=5 pilot, so mediation versus sham cannot be tested.
Reported resting theta and alpha changes but no control group, and theta moved opposite to the trained direction.

gap.why_it_matters_en: Without target engagement, cognitive gains in MCI could be placebo or practice effects, undermining the mechanistic rationale of reversing EEG slowing.
gap.severity_rationale_en: Attribution of effect to NF is the fundamental validity question for the whole field.
gap.novelty_rationale_en: Recognised in reviews but not yet addressed empirically in MCI; partially examined in other populations.
gap.feasibility_rationale_en: Standard EEG and mediation analysis; requires adequate sample size and a credible sham.

summary.executive_en: The collection shows that EEG neurofeedback in MCI yields promising but fragile, domain-specific cognitive gains from small and mostly uncontrolled studies. Three gaps stand out: (1) responder prediction and personalization have been studied only in healthy, middle-aged or subjective-decline samples, never in MCI; (2) no sham-controlled MCI trial has shown that the trained EEG feature actually changes and mediates the cognitive benefit; and (3) no completed MCI trial follows patients beyond about one month or measures clinical progression.
summary.coverage_en: Well covered: short-term cognitive effects of classic band protocols (alpha, beta, SMR/theta) in MCI (LavyEtAl2021; JirayucharoensakEtAl2019; MarlatsEtAl2020), multiple systematic and narrative reviews (TrambaiolliEtAl2021; TsaiEtAl2025; Tazaki2024; VilouEtAl2023), and emerging work on self-regulation failure in aging (MarcosMartinezEtAl2026; PabanEtAl2024).
summary.methodology_en: 9 experimental and 6 review papers; there are no computational, observational, engineering or theoretical papers. Experimental work is dominated by single-arm pilots and small trials; only one sham-controlled RCT in MCI (LavyEtAl2021).
summary.patterns_en: All three gaps stem from small, short, single-site designs that report averaged cognitive outcomes. Responder prediction (gap 1) and target-engagement mediation (gap 2) can be addressed jointly in one sham-controlled trial, which is a prerequisite for the long-term progression studies of gap 3.
